turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me a little bit about what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Um, well, I guess what finally pushed me to make this appointment is... work. I'm an auditor, and lately, I just keep starting these follow-up items after my audits, or after these mentorship events we run. And I have every intention of finishing them, I really do! But then I find out, you know, days later, that the final email or the review note or the official form never actually got done. 

Which is just so frustrating because I was just telling my mentee, Sarah—she's new, just moved here from Chicago, actually. Have you ever been? I went there for an accounting conference a few years ago and the wind off the lake is just brutal in November, but the pizza really is as good as they say. Deep dish isn't usually my favorite, I prefer a thin crust, but anyway... what was I saying? 

Right, the mentorship stuff. I was supposed to submit her feedback form, and I swear I started it, but then I got an email about the new parking garage rules at our building. They're changing the assigned spots again, which is a whole nightmare because my car barely fits in the compact spaces as it is, and the property manager is just impossible to get on the phone. But yeah, I'll start things with every intention of wrapping them up, and then days go by and I realize I never actually hit send on the email or finished the review.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly states they start workplace tasks like follow-up items, emails, and forms, but fail to finish them.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted from their work task by an extraneous stimulus (an email about parking garage rules).
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting off-topic to talk about Chicago, weather, and pizza before losing their train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your time in school, did you experience these same challenges with finishing tasks or staying on track?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. It goes way back. Even in elementary school, my report cards always said I was a bright kid, but I constantly lost my assignments. Which is funny to think about now, because my niece just got her report card last week, and they do it all online through this parent portal thing. It's so high-tech! When I was her age, it was that heavy cardstock paper, you know? And you had to physically get it signed and bring it back. My dad always signed mine with this specific blue fountain pen he bought on a trip to Germany. He was totally obsessed with that pen, he wouldn't let anyone else touch it... um, wait, what was I talking about? 

Oh, school. Right. So, yeah, the teachers would always write in the comments that I rushed past all the small details, and that I talked out of turn a lot. I guess I still do that! But they always noted that I needed constant reminders to actually finish my work. My mother still jokes about it to this day, actually. She always says I was the kind of kid who could completely ace a test without even trying, but then I'd fail the project because I'd just forget it was sitting right there in the bottom of my backpack.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient states that teachers noted they 'rushed past all the small details.'
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions needing 'constant reminders to actually finish my work.'
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports they 'constantly lost my assignments' in school.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by unrelated thoughts about their niece's report card and father's pen, losing their train of thought mid-sentence.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes forgetting that a completed project was sitting in the bottom of their backpack.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient notes that they 'talked out of turn a lot' in class and still do.

turns.doctor_question: Do you currently find yourself feeling physically restless, like you have an internal motor that won't turn off, or do you find that you frequently interrupt others when they are speaking?
turns.patient_response:
Well, the restless thing... I don't know if it's like a motor, exactly, but I definitely do the interrupting thing. I catch myself jumping into conversations all the time before people even finish their sentences. Especially with the junior auditors, like Sarah. It's just that the answer or the idea pops into my head and it feels so urgent, like I have to say it right that second, so I just blurt it out before I can even stop myself. 

Which I know is annoying! My ex-husband used to hate it when I did that. We'd be at dinner, trying to decide what to eat, and he'd be halfway through suggesting Thai food, and I'd just talk right over him about the new Italian place downtown. Speaking of Italian, have you tried that new spot on 4th Street? Bella something? The garlic knots are incredible, but they charge for extra marinara sauce, which I think is just ridiculous. Like, tomato sauce isn't that expensive to make! I actually tried making my own marinara from scratch last summer when my neighbor gave me all these extra tomatoes from her garden. She grows the big heirlooms, they're gorgeous, but the squirrels keep eating them off the vine before they're fully ripe. She put up this netting, but those squirrels are so smart, they just chew right through it. 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, right, interrupting. Yeah, I definitely do that a lot. I really try not to, but the thoughts just come so fast and I feel like if I don't say them immediately, they'll just vanish.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, going on a long tangent about Italian food and squirrels before forgetting the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they 'blurt it out' when an answer or idea pops into their head before they can stop themselves.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient confirms they frequently interrupt others, jumping into conversations before people finish their sentences.
symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient describes experiencing racing thoughts, stating that 'the thoughts just come so fast' and will vanish if not spoken immediately.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Beyond the tendency to interrupt others, do you often find yourself physically unable to sit still, such as feeling the need to constantly fidget, tap your feet, or pace around the room when you are expected to be sitting?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I guess I do have a hard time just... sitting. Like, especially in meetings. We have these endless partner meetings on Tuesday mornings, and I'm always doing something. Usually, I'm tapping my foot under the table, or I'm clicking my pen over and over. I actually had to stop bringing the clicky pens to the conference room because one of the senior partners gave me this look once. Now I try to just bring the ones with caps, but then I end up chewing on the cap or taking it on and off. 

My colleague, Dave—he sits next to me in most of these meetings—he actually joked the other day that he can hear my leg going before he even sees me. Dave's great, though. He just got a new puppy, a golden retriever mix, I think? He showed me pictures and it's so cute. It has these giant paws, so you know it's going to be huge. I had a golden when I was a kid, named Buster. Best dog ever, but the shedding was out of control. My mom was always vacuuming. She went through three vacuums in like, five years. She finally bought one of those really expensive German ones... wait, sorry. 

What was I saying? Oh, fidgeting. Yeah, I'm always shifting in my chair or moving my leg. It just feels like if I sit totally still, my skin starts crawling or something.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, going on a tangent about a colleague's puppy and childhood dogs before losing their train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly confirms tapping their foot, clicking pens, and constantly shifting in their chair during meetings.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an internal feeling of restlessness, stating that their 'skin starts crawling' if they try to sit totally still.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: When you are in those meetings or other quiet settings, do you often find yourself feeling an internal need to get up and leave your seat, or do you find that you frequently pace around the room even when you are expected to stay seated?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, completely. If I have to sit still for a long audit review or something, it actually starts to feel physically uncomfortable. It's exactly like you said, it's like this pressure building up inside me until I just absolutely have to stand up. I'll usually invent a reason to move, like going to get more coffee or walking over to the printer. 

Which, honestly, our main office printer is a total nightmare right now. It jams if you even look at it funny. We've had the IT guy, Kevin, look at it like five times this month alone. Kevin's an interesting guy, actually. He just started brewing his own kombucha and he leaves these weird glass jars of it in the breakroom fridge. It smells a little like vinegar, to be honest. I tried making kombucha once during lockdown, but I accidentally killed the SCOBY thing. You have to keep it at a very specific temperature, and my apartment is so drafty because the windows are from the 1920s. They have that beautiful original molding, but terrible insulation. My heating bill in January was completely outrageous... 

Um, sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, leaving my seat! Right. Yeah, so during those long reviews, the pressure just builds and builds. If I don't invent an excuse to get up and walk around for a minute, I feel like I'm going to jump out of my skin.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being distracted by a chain of unrelated thoughts (the printer, a coworker, kombucha, their apartment) and loses track of the original conversation topic.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient admits to inventing excuses, such as getting coffee or checking the printer, to leave their seat during long audit reviews where they are expected to remain seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes a physical discomfort and internal pressure building up, making them feel like they will 'jump out of my skin' if they cannot move.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Have these struggles with fidgeting, the need to move, and interrupting others been happening consistently for at least the past six months?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, definitely longer than six months. It's been noticeably interfering for, gosh, about a year and ten months now? Yeah, almost two years. It really started getting bad right after I got this big promotion. I had just won this firm-wide award, which was completely unexpected, honestly. They had this whole dinner for it and gave me this gorgeous engraved glass plaque. 

I actually keep the plaque on my desk right next to my spider plant. I love that plant, it's been throwing off little babies like crazy lately. I've been propagating them in these cute little glass yogurt jars and giving them out to the team. Sarah—the junior auditor I was talking about earlier—she somehow managed to kill hers in less than a week. I honestly don't know how you kill a spider plant, they're practically indestructible! You just give them a little water on Fridays. Though, to be fair, the water from our office tap tastes really metallic, so maybe the plant didn't like it. I started bringing in my own filtered water from home in this huge Hydro Flask because I just couldn't stand the taste of the office water anymore. Plus, those bottles keep ice cold for like, twenty-four hours, which is amazing... 

Wait, I'm sorry, I completely lost my train of thought again. You asked how long it's been happening. Right. So, yeah, about a year and ten months. Ever since that promotion after the award, my workload and all my new responsibilities have just been so much harder to juggle, and that's when I really noticed I couldn't sit still or stop interrupting people.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by going on a long tangent about plants and water bottles, explicitly stating they 'completely lost my train of thought'.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient confirms the doctor's question regarding their ongoing struggles with fidgeting.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms the doctor's question about the need to move, explicitly stating they 'couldn't sit still'.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient confirms the doctor's question about interrupting others, noting they couldn't 'stop interrupting people'.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
